#2062. Chelsea’s interest in Alex Scott remains despite Bournemouth transfer stance

Gary Gowers is a sports journalist and the editor of Read Everton, where he leads daily coverage of Everton news, transfers and analysis. He also writes about Manchester City for Read Man City and motorsport for Read Motorsport. A former accountant, he became a freelance writer in 2011 and has written for BBC Sport and Metro.

Bournemouth’s determination to keep Alex Scott has done little to discourage Chelsea, who remain among the leading contenders to sign the England midfielder.

The Blues had a £64m bid rejected during the summer, but their interest has continued into the new season. According to Matt Law of The Telegraph, Chelsea are at the front of the queue of clubs monitoring the 23-year-old.

Bournemouth, however, have no intention of allowing Scott to leave in January. talkSPORT reported this week that the south coast club remain determined to retain him, despite his reluctance to sign a contract extension.

Scott’s current deal runs until 2028, leaving Bournemouth with time to negotiate, although their position could become more complicated if no agreement is reached before next summer.

The midfielder’s immediate priority is recovering from a thigh injury sustained while representing England. He impressed during the 7-0 Nations League victory over Croatia but was withdrawn after 70 minutes. Subsequent examinations revealed a quadriceps problem, with BBC Sport reporting that he could miss six to eight weeks.

His absence is a setback for Bournemouth, who have relied heavily on the former Bristol City midfielder this season. It also introduces another consideration for clubs monitoring his progress ahead of the January window.

Chelsea are not alone in their admiration. Arsenal and Liverpool have also been linked with Scott, whose performances have attracted attention beyond the Premier League.

Suggestions circulating on social media that Bournemouth have already agreed to let him leave in January remain unsubstantiated. There has been no reliable confirmation of such an arrangement, and the club’s reported position is firmly against a winter sale.

For Chelsea, the more realistic opportunity may come next summer, particularly if Scott continues to resist signing a new contract.

#2061. These 10 questions to be answered on Newcastle United recruitment and Matthias Jaissle

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

I have been thinking about Matthias Jaissle and Newcastle United recruitment in recent times.

This comes after reading a few articles recently about Premier League managers who have lost their jobs over the past 18 months.

What really struck me was how often changing the manager appears to have made remarkably little difference.

Tottenham, unfortunately, are beginning to look a bit more coherent. It’s early days, but it does look like they’re improving. This got me thinking to what have they done differently, and importantly, what can Newcastle United learn from it?

The first obvious answer is they’ve spent a lot of money. But then, so have we…

Tottenham spent around £313 million (according to the various reports) in the summer transfer window, compared with Newcastle United’s £268 million (based on the various reporting).

Not an insignificant difference but hardly a world apart either.

Dig a little deeper, though, and there’s a fundamental difference between spending hundreds of millions on established Premier League players and spending hundreds of millions on players you hope will eventually become established Premier League players.

I think this distinction goes a long way towards explaining where we find ourselves today.

My first, and fairly obvious question, is…

Has recruitment been good enough at Newcastle United?

For me, the answer is no. Not even close!

Newcastle United have lost four world-class players in the last 18 months: Alexander Isak, Bruno Guimarães, Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali.

These were players operating at the highest level of the Premier League and proven international footballers. That is a ridiculous amount of quality to remove from any team. Then have a look at what we’ve brought in.

Not just this summer, but across the last couple of transfer windows. Newcastle United have thrown enormous amounts of money at Yoane Wissa, Anthony Elanga and Nick Woltemade, the latter being our record signing.

We’ve subsequently loaned Nick Woltemade to Juventus, where he’s barely able to establish himself in the first team. On top of that, we’ve brought in a number of young players who have very limited senior first-team experience anywhere in the world, never mind the Premier League.

This isn’t to suggest they’re not good enough. Some of them may turn out to be excellent. Sean Steur, for me, is the outstanding prospect of this group. But you have to recognise there’s a difference between potential and proven quality.

Potential doesn’t win you matches tomorrow.

Of our summer signings, I’d argue that González and Dedić were the two obvious first-team-ready acquisitions, both of whom appear to have been Matthias Jaissle picks. Dedić is still adjusting, but there’s certainly a very good player in there.

González is a bit more complicated. His passing range is excellent, but he’s glacially slow, struggles to beat opponents and relies heavily on movement ahead of him to be effective. Something he had in spades at Manchester City… At Newcastle United? Not so much. Watch him when he receives the ball. He looks up, searches for a forward pass and, more often than not, finds four attacking players standing there looking at him. When somebody actually makes a run through the channels, we’ve seen what he can do. Some of our better goalscoring opportunities have come from precisely those situations. His limitations are very real (comparisons to Rodri are laughable), but I think they’re also exaggerated by the lack of movement from the players ahead of him.

That’s a problem for Matthias Jaissle to solve.

Next, look at the balance of the squad. We spent heavily on Touré, a left winger, when we already have Barnes, who is very difficult to drop because he’s practically our only consistent source of goals. Also, at the sort of money we’re spending, surely we should be recruiting players capable of going straight into the first team?

Meanwhile, on the right, we’re still playing Jacob Murphy. I personally like Murphy, but he’s not getting any younger, and we’re hardly addressing the long-term problem by continuing to rely on him. At this point, though, I’m not sure we’ve got many options, aside from Elanga, who, for me, simply isn’t a particularly good footballer. He’s incredibly quick but his technical ability is poor. Yet another example of a very expensive signing that hasn’t delivered what we needed.

Then there’s Bamba. We spent £30 million, potentially rising to £36 million, on a young defensive midfielder when we were absolutely desperate for someone “ready to go” in that position. He hasn’t started a league match.

We have thrown an enormous amount of money at goalkeepers, young midfielders and attacking prospects, but we haven’t assembled a balanced first eleven. We continue to buy players for the future when we actually need players who can play now.

Are Newcastle United recruiting players to build a functioning football team, or are we acquiring footballers the recruitment department believes might become valuable assets at some point in the future?

They are two very different things and they lead to two very different outcomes on the pitch this season.

Back to Tottenham then and what have they done differently?

Take a look at at their recruitment this summer. Yes, I know they’ve spent a lot of money. Around £313 million, compared with our £268 million – but look at what they’ve bought.

Tonali, Fernandes, Sávio and Van Hecke are all established senior professionals with significant experience of playing at a high level in the Premier League. They knew what they were buying – first team ready players. It’s not just those four. The players they’ve recruited are, in general, capable of contributing immediately. They’ve also added several experienced players on free transfers, which to me, seems like a pretty solid transfer strategy, particularly if you’ve got a team whose first eleven needs strengthening today. The difference is that Tottenham have spent heavily on established players. We’ve spent heavily on potential and development projects. That distinction matters.

When we compare the money spent by the two clubs and conclude that their managers have been given equivalent resources, I think we are missing the point. They haven’t been given equivalent resources. They’ve been given players at very different stages of their careers, with very different levels of experience and readiness to perform in the Premier League.

Has Matthias Jaissle been given enough time?

In my view, absolutely not. The bloke arrived 18 days before the Premier League season started and he has subsequently managed ten league matches and pretty much achieved the same outcomes as we did last season. However, in that time, he’s been trying to implement a substantial tactical change, moving from a 4-3-3 to a 4-2-3-1 with a double pivot, whilst arguably, losing our best three players over the summer. This is a change that, as recently as the end of last season, plenty of us were crying out for.

Hindsight is a wonderful thing, but people on The Mag cannot seriously tell me that moving away from Eddie Howe’s 4-3-3 wasn’t one of the main topics of conversation for months. We wanted change. Well, now we’ve got it. And it needs time to be embedded.

This isn’t a minor tactical adjustment either. It significantly changes the responsibilities of the midfielders, the movement of the attacking players and the way we operate both in and out of possession. Add to that the fact that Matthias Jaissle is trying to teach this system to a squad containing several young players who are also adapting to a new club, a new league and, in some cases, a new country. Yes, of course, we’re not playing European football, I hear you say. And we’ve had the international breaks.

Well, not really is my view. When you account for the players away on international duty, then add the injury list, Jaissle is practically left with a five-a-side team to train. What’s he supposed to do? Run tactical classroom sessions with players recovering from torn tendons while the remaining five have a kickabout in the backyard? My view is that international breaks don’t do us any favours. If anything, they disrupt the rhythm of the team and what Jaissle is trying to achieve.

I’m not suggesting he should be given unlimited time. But judging him after ten matches, under these circumstances, seems ridiculous.

Does Matthias Jaissle have tactical responsibility?

Of course he does – and I believe criticism of the manager in this area is entirely legitimate.

The 4-2-3-1 has exposed some significant weaknesses in our midfield. In particular, our number ten is absolutely critical in that system. In my view, it is a linchpin role. That role needs to contribute to midfield, provide an additional passing option, press when needed and help prevent the two deeper midfielders from being overwhelmed.

What the number ten does both in and out of possession is fundamental to making the system work.

So what are we doing? We’re effectively playing a second striker there – often Wissa, sometimes Willock and neither of them are up to that role. What we’re seeing is the double pivot becoming isolated far too often. Opposition teams create numerical advantages in central midfield, and our attacking players become disconnected from the players trying to supply them.

Matthias Jaissle has to solve that problem.

Does that mean he should abandon the system? No, I don’t think so. It’s the football he wants us to play, and I think we need to be patient while the players learn it. The alternative is to abandon the approach after ten games and start again. I’m not entirely convinced that would benefit us either. We’ve seen plenty of clubs do precisely that. Sack the manager, appoint somebody with a different philosophy, recruit another collection of players.

Rinse and repeat. At some point, you have to commit to a direction and for me, that means committing to Matthias Jaissle and the system he’s trying to establish – that said, I do think he needs to show a bit more tactical flexibility.

As I’ve already said, the number ten is critical in this formation and Wissa or Willock are not the answer to that problem. In my view, we need two players in January: a proper number nine (obviously!) and a genuine number ten who can transition between midfield and attack, both in and out of possession – someone who can help the midfield when we’re under pressure and support the striker when we’re attacking. Getting this right needs time, and it needs players capable of executing the system.

Have Newcastle United actually got a recruitment strategy?

I keep coming back to this, and the answer almost invariably seems to be that, if we have one, it isn’t a particularly good one.

Dedić and González appear to have been recruited with Jaissle’s approval. Most of the other summer acquisitions arrived before he was appointed. We’ve effectively assembled a squad for one set of circumstances, appointed a manager who wants to play a different system, and then expected everything to come together almost immediately. And, if I am being honest, this isn’t a problem confined to one transfer window.

Look at the money we’ve spent over the past two years. Look at the players we’ve bought, the positions we’ve prioritised, the players we’ve subsequently moved on and the gaps that still exist in the squad – Financially, we simply cannot continue doing this. We don’t have the revenue to keep making these sorts of expensive mistakes and we now appear to be in a position where we can’t even recover the fees we’ve spent by selling some of these players.

Who’s going to pay the sort of money we paid for Wissa or Woltemade or Elanga? The answer is probably nobody.

Poor Newcastle United recruitment has consequences.

And right now, we’re seeing those consequences. It restricts what we can do in subsequent transfer windows. It limits our ability to strengthen the positions that genuinely need attention, particularly the number nine and number ten. And it ultimately leaves Jaissle trying to fit square pegs into round holes.

Jaissle has inherited a squad that has lost an extraordinary amount of established quality, has been assembled at enormous expense, and still appears poorly balanced and more focused on the future than today.

This is not his doing. It’s the consequence of the club’s recruitment strategy and replacing Jaissle won’t automatically resolve it.

These are the questions I’ve been pondering.

Has Newcastle United recruitment been good enough?

Does Matthias Jaissle still have tactical responsibilities?

But there’s a fourth question, and for me it’s the most important.

If we gave Matthias Jaissle another £150 million tomorrow, would the club actually have a coherent plan for spending it?

Looking at what we’ve bought over the past two years, the positions we’ve failed to strengthen and the quality we’ve allowed to leave, I think the answer is a resounding no.

And this worries me considerably more than whether our manager  Matthias Jaissle has got a perfectly balanced formation after ten games.

#2060. Arsenal Women vs Barcelona: Arsenal show their resilience with impressive draw against Barcelona

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal Women vs Barcelona: Arsenal Women claimed a vital point at the Camp Nou. They drew 1-1 against Barcelona in the Champions League on Thursday night.

Frida Maanum gave the Gunners the lead in the first half. Caroline Graham Hansen scored to bring the game level after the break. Whilst Renee Slegers will be disappointed to miss out on all three points, her side played some encouraging football.

Despite needing to play differently, Arsenal had an even game against an opposition who would inevitably have long periods of the ball. The visitors played very well defensively and looked dangerous when they could attack.

The result showed that Slegers has a team that can adapt to new challenges. This could be important for Arsenal as they try to make a mark in Europe.

One of the key decisions made by Slegers was to include Maanum. She had only recently returned from injury but made an impressive impact against Barcelona.

The midfielder scored early on to start the game in the right direction. Slegers was very impressed with her play when not in possession. She was praised for her communication skills and assisting others.

Arsenal’s attacking play was mainly based on fast counter attacks. They knew they wouldn’t be able to play in the same style as Barcelona and therefore tried to take advantage of the space on offer.

However, there were chances created in both halves. Arsenal may have been more clinical with their chances, they were always a threat.

Eventually, Barcelona scored their equaliser through Graham Hansen. Slegers said that Arsenal lost their shape during the move, which gave Hansen too much space.

It was a reminder of how quickly Barcelona can strike if you lose your concentration for a moment.

The Arsenal manager was pleased with the way her players implemented the game plan, showing tenacity, discipline, good communication and bravery.

Slegers admitted Arsenal did lose the ball too much in the second half, and by keeping it longer, they would have taken the pressure off defending against Barca’s dangerous attack.

There was some frustration that Arsenal couldn’t hold onto their lead, and there were more chances created towards the end of the game. The visitors got into good positions to win corners but couldn’t get the winning goal.

They will feel very positive from their display. They put themselves up against one of the biggest tests in the Camp Nou and proved that they can cause Barcelona problems.

There isn’t much time to really reflect on the result ahead of their game against the London City Lionesses on Sunday, but Slegers now has another example of what her side can do when they play with purpose and structure.

#2059. Chelsea make early move for Palmeiras teenager Eduardo Conceicao

Gary Gowers is a sports journalist and the editor of Read Everton, where he leads daily coverage of Everton news, transfers and analysis. He also writes about Manchester City for Read Man City and motorsport for Read Motorsport. A former accountant, he became a freelance writer in 2011 and has written for BBC Sport and Metro.

Chelsea have reportedly made contact with Palmeiras as they attempt to gain an early advantage in the race to sign Brazilian teenager Eduardo Conceicao.

The 16-year-old forward has attracted attention from several leading European clubs, but Chelsea are understood to be among the first to establish direct contact with Palmeiras over a potential future transfer.

According to Mark Brus of CaughtOffside, the London club have held a series of discussions as they seek to position themselves ahead of their rivals.

Palmeiras are reportedly preparing for substantial offers, with some figures at the Brazilian club discussing a valuation as high as €100m (£85m).

That figure has not been established as a firm asking price, however, and Brus reports that industry sources expect the eventual cost to be lower. Chelsea’s previous investment of approximately £51m in Estevao is regarded as a possible benchmark.

Manchester City’s ownership group have also made contact regarding Conceicao, while Arsenal, Manchester United, Barcelona, Real Madrid, Bayern Munich and Paris Saint-Germain are among the clubs reported to have watched him.

Chelsea’s existing relationship with Palmeiras could help their efforts, although the level of competition means there is no guarantee that their early interest will lead to a deal.

The player’s age is another consideration. Conceicao cannot complete an international transfer to England until he turns 18, leaving interested clubs facing a potentially lengthy wait before he can join their squads.

Chelsea have already demonstrated their willingness to agree deals for young players well before they are eligible to arrive, with Estevao providing a particularly relevant example.

No formal bid or agreement has been reported for Conceicao. Nevertheless, the latest claims suggest Chelsea are prepared to explore another long-term investment in Brazilian talent rather than wait until the player becomes available for an immediate move.

#2058. West Ham Fanzine Blowing Bubbles Shortlisted for National Award

West Ham might be lumbering in mid-table but Hammers fanzine Blowing Bubbles is very much top of class after it was shortlisted for Fanzine of the Year at the 2026 Football Supporters’ Association Awards.

It’s the fourth time the publication has received the recognition, having previously been nominated in 2015, 2021 and 2023. Blowing Bubbles joins five other finalists, including Sunderland’s A Love Supreme, Leeds United’s The Square Ball and Middlesbrough’s Fly Me To The Moon.

Editor David Blackmore launched Blowing Bubbles in the summer of 2012 and has been involved ever since. The publication celebrated its 100th edition in February 2020 and has now reached issue 173, which is quite an achievement for an independent monthly football fanzine.

“I’m absolutely delighted that Blowing Bubbles has been shortlisted for Fanzine of the Year for a fourth time. To be in such an elite group of fantastic football publications is a massive pat on the back and recognition of not only the huge amount of time and effort we put into producing every issue but also to the continued support we’ve had from the West Ham Family.”

Anyone involved in producing independent football content will appreciate the work that goes into keeping a publication going month after month. Credit must also go to David’s team of writers and designer Kelvin Farrell.

The winners will be announced on Monday 30 November at London’s Nobu, Portman Square, with Victoria Derbyshire hosting the FSA Awards. The fanzine category will be decided by a judging panel.

From all of us at Claret & Hugh, congratulations to David and the entire Blowing Bubbles team. Best of luck on awards night. Fingers crossed you bring the trophy home!

Kris Gonzo (commonly known to the West Ham community as Gonzo) is the co-founder of Hammers Chat (established 2014) and the lead video content creator and columnist for Claret and Hugh.

With over a decade of professional sports media experience, he is a frequent West Ham United analyst and contributor for Sky Sports News, BBC Football Focus, and BBC Radio 5 Live. He previously served as an official video and content creator for West Ham United FC during the club's tenure at Upton Park and featured in the official documentary commemorating the historic final game at the Boleyn Ground.

A lifelong Hammer since the legendary 10-0 victory over Bury, when he isn't providing daily match analysis on the Hammers Chat YouTube Channel or broadcasting on X (@GONZObignose), he can be found walking his dog and restoring classic pinball machines.

#2056. Alan Shearer explains why Ezri Konsa has impressed him

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Alan Shearer believes Ezri Konsa has been the Premier League’s best player this season after an impressive start to his Arsenal career.

But the former Newcastle United striker has been impressed by the Gunners’ backline and feels Konsa should take a large amount of credit for the fact that they have not missed William Saliba so much.

Konsa’s arrival at Emirates has provided Mikel Arteta with a defender, but his performances have caused some issues for the Arsenal boss. Konsa is now a viable option for Arteta to play, as Saliba is fit again.

Shearer feels Konsa has done enough to be regarded as the best player in the division so far.

He stated in the Metro that Konsa has been effective while playing for Arsenal in the defence.

The former Newcastle player believed that Konsa has been the best player in the Premier League during this season. He pointed out the proof of the performance in the defence, arguing that people did not notice the missing Saliba until now.

Konsa has proved just how much he has grown since moving to the Emirates. Arsenal have been very strong at the back with Konsa playing a massive part.

But there is a problem with Konsa’s performances. Even if Saliba is fit he has done more than enough to make his place difficult to take.

Saliba is still one of Arsenal’s most important defenders, so Arteta will be delighted to have him back. However, he can’t ignore what Konsa has done in his absence.

It would be a tough call to leave the Englishman out, as he has been in such great form. But it means an experienced first choice defender would be left on the bench.

Konsa and Saliba could make a good partnership if they are given time to understand each other on the pitch. They will need to play regularly to do this.

Konsa has made it very hard not to pick him. He has been performing so well that he has created a dilemma for the manager.

Shearer highlights how well he has done by saying this. Arteta will have to figure out how to make the most out of his two quality defenders.

#2055. Chelsea news: Stewart departure, Scott interest and Bournemouth preparations

Gary Gowers is a sports journalist and the editor of Read Everton, where he leads daily coverage of Everton news, transfers and analysis. He also writes about Manchester City for Read Man City and motorsport for Read Motorsport. A former accountant, he became a freelance writer in 2011 and has written for BBC Sport and Metro.

Chelsea’s sporting department is facing another change following news of Laurence Stewart’s impending departure, while the club continue to be linked with potential additions to their squad.

Alex Scott and Palmeiras teenager Eduardo Conceicao have both featured in Thursday’s transfer coverage, with Xabi Alonso also preparing his players for Saturday’s Premier League meeting with Bournemouth.

Here is our 7pm round-up of the latest Chelsea news for Thursday, 8 October.

Laurence Stewart is set to leave Chelsea by mutual consent after almost four years at Stamford Bridge, with the club planning to redistribute his responsibilities rather than appoint a direct replacement.

His departure is understood to be amicable and will not take immediate effect. Stewart joined from Monaco in 2022, initially as technical director, before becoming co-sporting director alongside Paul Winstanley.

As detailed in our report on Stewart’s departure and Chelsea’s leadership reshuffle, Winstanley, Sam Jewell and Joe Shields are expected to take on expanded responsibilities across recruitment, player development and the wider BlueCo operation.

The changes follow discussions about the club’s sporting structure that reportedly began earlier this year. There is no confirmed suggestion that Stewart’s departure resulted from a disagreement with Alonso.

Chelsea’s reported interest in Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott remains a talking point, despite the south coast club’s determination to retain the England international.

The Blues reportedly had a £64m offer rejected during the summer, with Matt Law of The Telegraph subsequently identifying Chelsea as leading contenders for the 23-year-old.

However, as examined in our latest report on Chelsea’s interest in Scott, Bournemouth are not expected to entertain a January sale.

Scott’s immediate concern is recovering from a thigh injury suffered while representing England. The midfielder could face several weeks on the sidelines, potentially complicating Bournemouth’s plans as well as any future discussions about his next move.

Chelsea have also reportedly made contact with Palmeiras over 16-year-old forward Eduardo Conceicao, who is attracting attention from several leading European clubs.

According to Mark Brus of CaughtOffside, Chelsea have held discussions with the Brazilian club as they explore the possibility of a future deal.

Our report on Chelsea’s interest in Eduardo Conceicao explains that a valuation as high as €100m has been suggested, although that figure is not a confirmed asking price or evidence of a formal bid.

Manchester City, Arsenal and Real Madrid are among the other clubs reportedly monitoring the teenager. Conceicao would be unable to complete a transfer to England until he turns 18, making any prospective move a longer-term consideration.

Alonso’s attention will now turn to Saturday’s Premier League meeting with Bournemouth at Stamford Bridge.

The match kicks off at 3pm and will not be televised live in the United Kingdom because of the Saturday afternoon broadcasting blackout.

Our Chelsea v Bournemouth kick-off and how-to-watch guide provides the full details, including how to follow the match and the available overseas broadcast information.

Scott’s injury is expected to deprive Bournemouth of an important midfield option, although Chelsea will have their own fitness decisions to make as players return from international duty.

After Saturday’s fixture, Chelsea travel to Hill Dickinson Stadium to face Everton on 17 October. Alonso will be looking for greater consistency as the domestic programme resumes.
